doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Arriving at Eastman as a self-taught outsider
summary: At Eastman without a jazz program he was a back-door learner, and found local Rochester orchestra attitudes unappealing.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: And so I went to Eastman and I was just different than a lot of the people but I had good friends there you know.

Well that’s what I’m going to tell you. So most of them studied with orchestral people. There weren’t many jazz people there because they didn’t have a jazz program then. Jazz had to meet on Saturdays and you didn’t get credit for it. And you know so basically, you know it was I don’t want to say anti-jazz but it wasn’t part of the curriculum at first. I was there during the transition to having a wonderful jazz program. So I go there you know and they were all talking about my teacher said this. And I was the person, I’d say, “Man, what’s that trumpet you’re playing? Why did you cut off your tuning slide?” And they’d laugh. They said, “You never seen a C trumpet before?” “Well no” I said, “I’ve heard about C trumpet but I thought it just meant transpose up a step.” So you know what I mean? My whole growth was what do you call that, natural. It didn’t have any organization to it. My organization was there’s no trumpet in that. I wonder why there’s no trumpet in that. You know what I mean? I was back-door learning. I’d say, “Wow that’s a string group” and then I’d start studying, listening to these string quartets because I was interested. And when I played in the orchestra at Eastman I didn’t know anything about a lot of the instruments. I was a music ed major, thank goodness, because I took every instrument for a little bit and it helped me — actually it helped me to play with other people in the future. But so when I was in orchestra, you know it was like some of these people have a terrible attitude. Then I started playing extra, with a local orchestra in Rochester, and they seemed like, you know they were reading Golf Magazine when they had rests and stuff, and I’m going, “I like this music. I don’t think they like this music.” You know of course I’m young. So that’s my perception. And then I noticed sometimes they wouldn’t pay attention and it wouldn’t get — you know I don’t want to live in this little town 20 or 30 hours a week with this group. This is not my close group that I want to be in.
Isn’t it interesting that you can learn things from negative experiences.
